title: How LLMs work: tokens, context, sampling
summary: Understand how a large language model turns text into tokens, predicts the next one, and how context and sampling shape its output.
objectives: Explain what a token is and why models work in tokens, not words
Describe next-token prediction as the core mechanism of an LLM
Understand the context window and why it is a hard limit
Explain how temperature and top-p sampling control randomness
Connect tokens to cost, latency, and the max_tokens setting
Make a basic call to the Claude Messages API in Python

options: A common chunk of text, often part of a word
quiz.why: Tokens are sub-word chunks. A word like "unhappiness" may split into several tokens, while a common word is usually one.

quiz.q: At its core, what does a language model actually do?
options: Look answers up in a database
Predict the next token given the previous ones
Translate words into numbers and stop
quiz.why: An LLM is a next-token predictor. It repeatedly picks the most likely next token, then feeds it back in to continue.

quiz.q: What does the context window limit?
quiz.answer: The total number of tokens (input plus output) the model can consider at once.
quiz.why: Everything you send plus everything the model generates must fit inside the context window; older tokens beyond it are not seen.

quiz.q: What happens to randomness as you lower the temperature toward 0?
options: Output becomes more deterministic and focused
quiz.why: Low temperature sharpens the probability distribution, so the model almost always picks the most likely token, giving stable, repetitive output.

quiz.q: Why does token count matter in a real application?
quiz.answer: Tokens drive cost and latency, and both input and output count toward the context window and pricing.
quiz.why: APIs bill per token and longer prompts take longer to process, so counting tokens helps you control cost and stay within limits.

quiz.q: In the Claude Messages API, what does max_tokens control?
options: The size of the input prompt
The maximum number of tokens the model may generate in its reply
quiz.why: max_tokens caps the length of the model's response only; it does not limit the input you send.

body_markdown:
## Tokens: the model's units

A **large language model** does not read words the way you do. It reads **tokens** — common chunks of text. A token might be a whole short word, a piece of a longer word, a space, or a punctuation mark. As a rough rule, one token is about four characters of English, or roughly three quarters of a word.

The text is converted into tokens by a *tokenizer*, and each token maps to a number the model can do maths on. So before any prediction happens, your sentence becomes a list of integers.

## Next-token prediction

At its heart, an LLM does one thing: given the tokens so far, it predicts a **probability for every possible next token**. It then picks one, appends it, and repeats. That loop — predict, append, predict again — is how a whole paragraph gets generated, one token at a time.

This is why models sometimes "drift": each new token depends only on what came before, so a small early choice can steer the rest of the answer.

## The context window

The **context window** is the maximum number of tokens the model can hold in mind at once. Crucially, this budget covers **both** your input (the prompt) **and** the output it generates. If a conversation grows too long, the oldest tokens fall outside the window and the model simply cannot see them.

Think of it like working memory: large, but finite. Modern models have very large windows, but you still design prompts to fit.

## Sampling: temperature and top-p

The model gives a *distribution* over next tokens. **Sampling** decides how we pick from it.

- **Temperature** scales how sharp or flat the distribution is. Low temperature (near 0) makes output focused and near-deterministic; high temperature adds variety and surprise.
- **Top-p** (nucleus sampling) keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to *p*, then samples from those.

Low temperature for facts and code; higher for brainstorming and creative writing.

## Tokens, cost, and latency

Because work scales with tokens, **tokens are money and time**. APIs bill per input token and per output token, and longer prompts take longer to process. Counting tokens before sending helps you predict cost and stay inside the window.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

count = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How do tokens work?"}],
)
print(count.input_tokens)
```

## Your first Claude call

Here is a minimal call to the Claude Messages API. Note `max_tokens`: it caps the length of the **reply**, not your input.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain a token in one sentence."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

Keep your API key in an environment variable (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) — never hard-code it.

## Your task

Paste a sentence into a tokenizer tool and count the tokens. Then make the basic Claude call above and read the response.

A tool called a tokenizer turns your text into tokens, and each token becomes a number the model can do maths on.

slides.narration: At its heart, a language model does just one thing. Given the tokens so far, it predicts a probability for every possible next token. It picks one, adds it to the end, and then predicts again. That simple loop, repeated, is how a whole answer gets written, one token at a time. This is also why a small choice early on can steer the rest of the response.

slides.title: The context window
bullets: The max tokens the model holds at once.
Covers input AND output together.
Old tokens beyond it are not seen.
Like working memory: large but finite.
slides.narration: Every model has a context window: the maximum number of tokens it can hold in mind at one time. The important part is that this budget covers both your prompt and the reply the model generates. If a conversation grows too long, the oldest tokens fall outside the window, and the model simply cannot see them. Think of it as working memory, large but always finite.

slides.title: Sampling: temperature
bullets: The model outputs a distribution over tokens.
Temperature controls how sharp it is.
Low (near 0): focused, near-deterministic.
High: more variety and surprise.
slides.narration: When the model predicts the next token, it gives a whole distribution of possibilities. Sampling decides how we pick from it. Temperature is the main dial. A low temperature, near zero, makes the model almost always choose the most likely token, so output is focused and steady. A higher temperature flattens the choices, adding variety and surprise. Use low for facts and code, higher for creative work.

slides.title: Sampling: top-p
bullets: Top-p is nucleus sampling.
Keep smallest set of tokens summing to p.
Then sample only from that set.
Trims away unlikely tail options.
slides.narration: There's a second dial called top-p, or nucleus sampling. Instead of considering every token, it keeps only the smallest group of tokens whose probabilities add up to p, say zero point nine, and samples from just those. This trims away the unlikely tail of weird options while still allowing some variety. Temperature and top-p are often used together to shape the style of the output.

slides.title: Common misconceptions
bullets: It is not searching a database of answers.
It does not store your sentence as words.
Temperature 0 is steady, not 'smarter'.
max_tokens limits output, not the prompt.
slides.narration: Let's clear up a few traps. An L L M is not looking answers up in a database; it is predicting tokens. It does not keep your sentence as words; it keeps tokens, which are numbers. Temperature zero makes output steady and repeatable, but it does not make the model more intelligent. And max_tokens limits only how long the reply can be, not how long your prompt may be. Keep these straight and the rest of the month will click into place.

slides.narration: Let's recap. Models work in tokens, not words. Their core job is to predict the next token and repeat. The context window limits your input plus the output together. And temperature and top-p shape how random or focused the answer is.
